sections.h2: Selling a house in Oro Valley, AZ
sections.html:
Oro Valley belongs to Pima County, not Maricopa County, and the town runs its own short-term rental licensing. Expect different offices and forms than you would find in the Phoenix area. The town is in the foothills north of Tucson, and its housing market leans toward older, higher-income owners.

The July 2025 estimate is 48,085 residents, against 47,070 counted in 2020. A median owner-occupied home was worth $475,700 over 2020 to 2024. Owners live in 76.4 percent of homes, 35.7 percent of residents are 65 or older, and a typical household has 2.20 people. Plenty of owners spend only part of the year here, so your buyer or your co-owner may be reachable mostly by phone.

Some lots carry conservation easements, utility easements or floodplain areas that restrict where anything can be built. Read the survey and recorded easements before telling a buyer a pool or addition is possible.

For permit history on your house, phone the Community and Economic Development Department at 520-229-4800 or write to Permits@orovalleyaz.gov. Work on pools, spas, pool heaters and grading can require a permit, and the Planning Division will tell you whether a project meets zoning standards even when no permit applies.

Make a list of every improvement, including the ones you inherited from the previous owner, since the town's records follow the house and not the owner:

  • Additions, garages and remodels
  • A pool, spa or pool heater
  • Walls, sheds and grading

Raise any missing permit with the town promptly, before you receive an offer, because untangling it in the middle of escrow can push back closing.

Short-term rentals are allowed by right in all residential districts here. A homeowners association may still prohibit them, and the town licenses them under Ordinance (O)23-01. What a license takes:

  • An $80 fee, the same as a Town business license.
  • A state Transaction Privilege Tax license listing Oro Valley.
  • Registration with the Pima County Assessor under A.R.S. 33-1902.
  • Proof of liability insurance of at least $500,000, or a booking platform that provides equal coverage.
  • A neighbor notice, with the license number shown in rental ads.

Enforcement is by complaint rather than inspection. If your house has been a rental, give the buyer the license details and any HOA rental terms.

sections.h2: Recording the deed in Pima County
sections.html:
The Pima County Recorder files your deed along with an affidavit of property value, which you can get from the Arizona Department of Revenue. The flat recording charge is $30.00 per document under A.R.S. 11-475.

Two offices take documents: 240 N Stone Avenue downtown and 6920 E Broadway Blvd, Suite D. Valid photo identification is required of anyone filing in person under A.R.S. 11-472. Anything that arrives after 4 p.m. Tucson time waits for the next business day. In most sales the title company handles the filing and you never visit.

Pima County bills in two halves, with dates set by A.R.S. 42-18052.

Payment optionDue dateDelinquent after
First halfOctober 15:00 p.m. on November 1
Second halfMarch 15:00 p.m. on May 1
Bill of $100 or lessOctober 1, whole amountAfter December 31

Call the Pima County Treasurer to learn whether the first half on your parcel has been paid. At closing your title company allocates the year's bill to you and the buyer.

sections.h2: If taxes are owed or you live elsewhere
sections.html:
An unpaid first half will not stop a sale. Mention it to the title company at the outset, since the balance can come out of your proceeds at closing. A current figure from the Treasurer keeps the settlement statement free of surprises.

Part-year residents face a practical question: who signs, and where? Ask the title company early whether the deed can be signed away from home, and give them the mailing address you use while you are gone. The recorder requires photo identification for in-person filing, so the title company or a trusted representative may have to carry the paperwork.

If an HOA governs the house, ask its manager for resale paperwork the same week you decide to sell. Its rules on rentals may also matter to an investor buyer.

sections.h2: What a buyer will ask about
sections.html:
Expect questions in a predictable order. First comes the lot: where the house sits, what the easements allow and whether any floodplain touches it. Then the improvements: was the pool permitted, was the garage conversion inspected. After that, the rules: does the HOA allow rentals, and does the house carry a short-term rental license that a buyer would have to replace.

Last comes money. Buyers ask what the annual tax bill is, which half is paid and whether the HOA charges any special assessment. None of these answers is hard to find, but each one needs a phone call to a different office. Sellers who made the calls before listing tend to keep a contract together, because the buyer's questions get answered the same day.

Amphitheater Public Schools operates the public schools. Canyon del Oro High School and Ironwood Ridge High School are its high schools in town. Families can also look at BASIS Schools Oro Valley, Leman Academy of Excellence, Casas Christian School, Pusch Ridge Christian Academy and Immaculate Heart Preparatory School. Phone the district to learn which school a specific address is assigned to before quoting it to a buyer.

sections.h2: Steps for an Oro Valley seller
sections.html:
Most of the work comes before any contract is signed.

  1. Pull the survey and recorded easements and note anything that limits building.
  2. Call Community and Economic Development about permits for a pool, addition or remodel.
  3. If tenants or guests lived there, confirm the rental license, tax license and HOA terms.
  4. Locate your latest tax bill and ask the Treasurer what has been paid.
  5. Hand your title company what it needs to prepare the deed and affidavit.
  6. On closing day the title company files the deed in Pima County and releases proceeds after payoffs.

Cash offers skip the buyer's loan process and most showings. They do not erase permit questions or the recording, so finish those checks first. Ask the title company which pieces you can complete by phone and email and which require your signature in person.

After closing, keep your copy of the recorded deed and the settlement statement. If a question about the rental license or an old permit comes up later, those papers show what you handed over and when.

faqs.q: Do you need a license to rent a house short term in Oro Valley?
faqs.a: Yes. The town's license costs $80, and the owner also needs a state Transaction Privilege Tax license and a Pima County Assessor registration. An HOA can set stricter limits.

faqs.q: Which county records a deed for an Oro Valley house?
faqs.a: Pima County. The recorder charges $30.00 per document and asks for an affidavit of property value with the sale.

faqs.q: Do I need photo ID to record a document in Pima County?
faqs.a: Yes, if you file in person. The recorder asks for valid photo identification at the counter.

faqs.q: Who runs the public schools in Oro Valley?
faqs.a: Amphitheater Public Schools. Canyon del Oro and Ironwood Ridge are its high schools in the town. Check the assigned school for your address with the district.

faqs.q: When is the first-half property tax deadline?
faqs.a: October 1 is the due date, and the first half is delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on November 1. The second half is due March 1 and delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on May 1.
